utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I welcome you this Tuesday morning after a long break to everyone in the courtroom and those just outside the courtroom who are assisting us. Today has been scheduled as the first day for the closing argument. At least, I take it that the parties want to use the right to present closing argument, as the rule says, the Prosecution may present the closing argument. I take it, Mr. Ierace, that the Prosecution wants to present a closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, the Prosecution does exercise that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the Defence will also use its right to present its closing argument. I'd like to add one thing to that, that is, that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence do not provide specifically for what is known in the civil-law world as the last word, that means a statement by an accused speaking last at trial. Nevertheless, the Chamber is aware that in some cases, Chambers have been -- have granted the accused an opportunity to speak. If an application would be made to this extent, then the Chamber of course would first hear the Prosecution on whether they would oppose against the accused speaking last. But the Chamber indicates that it does not take an unfavourable attitude if such an application would be made. Then the scheduling of the closing arguments is such that the Chamber expects the Prosecution to close its arguments by today because we have approximately four hours effective time in Court. I might make a mistake, five hours, so that would bring us just a bit into tomorrow. Mr. Ierace, if you're ready to proceed, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, this accused stands charged with extraordinary crimes, which ultimately come down to this: That for 23 months, from September 1992, he ordered the deliberate targeting of the civilian inhabitants of a European city with the intention of terrorising its entire civilian population. In order to force its legitimate, internationally recognised government to capitulate. In so doing, not that it matters for the proof of the charges against him, the accused was in turn acting upon the orders of his immediate superior, General Ratko Mladic, and the Bosnian Serb political leadership. The indictment alleged a pattern of such conduct over that period, the indictment period, that can be characterised as a campaign. During the indictment period, within the Bosnian government lines, there lived 340.000 civilians. Many had escaped the city, but there had been a flow into it as well of refugees escaping the horrors in other parts of the former Yugoslavia. We heard statistical evidence that during the indictment period, those 23 months, some 1.185 civilians within the Bosnian government lines in Sarajevo were killed. And 4.701 civilians were wounded. The total of 5.886. The Prosecution submits that having regard to the totality of the evidence, a bare minimum of a thousand of those total civilian casualties can be accepted by the Trial Chamber as directly attributable to the accused's criminal behaviour as encapsulated in the charges against him. But all of those 340.000 civilians were victims of the first count in the indictment; namely, the infliction of terror for 23 months. The indictment makes clear that the scale of the complain was so great that the schedules of woundings and killings by sniping and shelling which are annexed to it are only a small representative number of the killings and woundings involved. The evidence of the pattern and the scale of the campaign emerged through the testimony of surviving victims and other eyewitnesses. It was confirmed by the testimony of experienced and qualified UN military observers who, at the time, detected behind the daily individual incidents the pattern and gave evidence of their conclusion and the observations which led to that inevitable conclusion. The Prosecution has, we submit, established a circumstantial case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt in relation to each of the charges against him. Our written submissions in some detail examine that circumstantial evidence that civilians were deliberately targeted and that the accused exercised command and control over his infantry and artillery assets that perpetrated the campaign on his behalf, indeed, on his orders. The inevitable conclusion is that the targeting could not have happened for so long and in a fashion which was observed to be responsive to his actions unless he had ordered it in the first place. That command and control was demonstrated in various ways, as articulated in our written submissions. The targeting would quickly stop whenever the accused or his senior subordinates agreed to cease-fire, or it would intensify to bring pressure to bear on the Bosnian government for a variety of reasons. We heard evidence of how on many occasions, the city would receive indiscriminate onslaughts in order to force the Bosnian government to stop an advance on the battlefield elsewhere in Bosnia. The UN senior military observer for the first three months of the accused's command, Lieutenant-Colonel Richard Mole said, "There was an accepted norm, that is, the Serb side failed to achieve their objectives and I use that in the widest context, so that could be anything, from a local complaint to something else that happened within Bosnia, the general perception was that Sarajevo would suffer as a result. This was always interpreted to mean that artillery fire would be brought to bear on the city in response. There were instances when this was quite specifically made as a threat." It reached the point that Lieutenant-Colonel Mole's morning briefing about events elsewhere in Bosnia alerted him to the possibility of repercussions within the Sarajevo sector. In such instances, he would speak with the accused with the objective of trying to prevent repercussions in Sarajevo in response to these outside events. Indeed, the primary evidence against the accused, though, is surely that of admissions made by him, direct evidence of his guilt. Evidence that he admitted he was indiscriminate firing into the city. He admitted it. His operational staff admitted it. His boss from whom he obtained his orders, General Mladic, admitted it. Mladic's staff admitted it. The accused's soldiers on the front line operating the very anti-aircraft guns, artillery, machine-guns, admitted it. Independent UN military observers witnessed SRK, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, crews indiscriminately firing into the city and admitting it, and they protested to the accused about it and related to the Chamber how he sought to justify it. If the Prosecution case consisted of just this evidence of admissions, then together with evidence that civilians were indeed targeted by his subordinates, it is an overwhelming, unanswerable case against the accused. As well as evidence of admissions by the accused, there was evidence of threats made by him and carried out. Threats to target civilians either directly or indiscriminately. Lieutenant-Colonel Mole said that he would be quite specifically told that Sarajevo would be shelled if the demands made on behalf of the Serb side were not met. He said that this type of threat was made by the accused five to ten times. He said he also received this type of threat from the accused's liaison officers. Accordingly, he said, "the city of Sarajevo which was to all intents and purposes in a hostage situation would be used as a counter pressure point for the events elsewhere in Sarajevo or Bosnia." As an example, he related a conversation in which the accused threatened to him that if the ABiH, the army of the Bosnian government, did not cease firing from Mount Igman there would be reciprocal firing by his weapons on to the city of Sarajevo. This evidence of admissions and threats by the accused demands a response. But where in the Defence's 270 pages of final written submissions does it deal with this evidence? With the exception of a few oblique sentences, it does not. Why? I suggest because that evidence is so persuasive, so determinative, so corroborated that there is no answer to it. It happened, the words were said, and the accused through his Defence has been unable to credibly explain it away. The accused chose to not enter the witness box and be cross-examined about this evidence. Instead, it was left to his former liaison officer, Colonel Indic, to deny some of those admissions, those which were made in his presence. But Colonel Indic was hardly in the best position to deny admissions made by the accused when he himself, according to the commander of the UN military observers on the SRK side of the confrontation lines, had confided in him hundreds of times that the targeting of civilians was part of the SRK plan. Mr. President, at this stage, one applies all the evidence, and in so doing, the evidence in relation to one part can be eliminating, indeed, corroborative, or complementary to another part of the Prosecution case. For example, the evidence of deliberate targeting of civilians with the use of professional sniper techniques and ordinary infantry weapons can be applied to the determination of what specifically was being targeted by the mortar and artillery assets of the SRK. Put simply, if the Trial Chamber is satisfied that civilians were being deliberately shot and that the shooters came under the same command as the mortar, anti-aircraft, and other artillery assets, that targeting evidence can be applied to the use of all assets. The Prosecution led evidence that there was a high level of coordination in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps which was, in turn, evidence of a high level of command and control by the SRK leadership, namely, the accused. In its written submissions, the Defence has not challenged the evidence to the effect that there was a high degree of coordination within the SRK at the level of its artillery and infantry assets and between those levels and the SRK command. Indeed, it is the Defence case as I perceive it as well that there was a high level of command and control by the accused. The difference is that whereas the Prosecution says that in conjunction with the evidence that the 23 months civilians were targeted by his forces, his strong command and control is evidence that he knew of this behaviour, sanctioned it, and indeed ordered it. The Defence says that his strong command and control is evidence that his orders that civilians were not to be targeted were carried out. We have heard in the trial evidence that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps controlled significant high points, high elevations, adjacent to the city centre. The sprawling slopes of Mount Trebevic to the South East, Sharpstone, Mrkovici, and Poljane to the northeast. But beyond those features, the SRK controlled the territory. Even to the north where the SRK did not control some of the immediate high ground over the city, such the hill Hum, they held such a depth of territory beyond it that they could bring their artillery to bear on the city from right around Sarajevo. The investigator Mr. Kucanin gave detail of sources of artillery and mortar as well as sniping fire around Sarajevo, right around Sarajevo. Mr. President, if all works well on our screens shortly, we should see a map. This is a map tendered by the Defence through, as I recollect, Dr. Radinovic, the military expert. The map demonstrates the degree to which Sarajevo was surrounded. It also demonstrates the depth of territory held by the SRK around the city. Given the range of the hundreds, if not thousands, of artillery pieces possessed by the SRK, it cannot be disputed that they were in a dominating position around the city. Sarajevo is seen towards the centre of the map; SRK territory to the right half of the map; ABiH territory to the left. From the perspective of the ABiH, the only way in or out of the city as demonstrated by the map was across the airport. It was hotly contested territory for that very good reason. Intermingled with the military who traversed the airport were civilians, either departing the city or returning to it. As a consequence, we have heard there were daily civilian casualties. UN military observer Tucker said, "another aspect of the civilians trying to run across the airport was that the Bosnian Serbs had set up snipers with night sights and machine guns with night sights, and they had fired at the civilians trying to run across the airport. And in January and February every night between 5 and 20 or 30 civilians were killed or injured by these snipers. And the Serb snipers were not particularly careful at what they sniped at, and they also killed and injured a number of the French soldiers who were trying to round up the escaping civilians to return them." The reference to January and February is 1993. The evidence was that that pattern continued for much of the indictment period. General Abdel Razek, senior UNPROFOR commander, protested to the accused about civilians being shot by his forces as they crossed this airfield. He said this issue was a source of friction and tension, and people, because of their difficulties, they used to take a great deal of risk in order to go and see their families, to be reunited with their family members. So a great deal of casualties did occur. And every day, we received reports telling us that a lady was killed with her child while she was trying to cross. Many casualties took place. There were exchanges of fire, but he said: "However, from the Serb side, it was more intensive. I do recall quite clearly that I put this matter to General Galic in one of our meetings." The accused, he said, was adamant on the fact that he will continue to stop this movement, crossing the airfield, by all means, using all means. As mentioned earlier, the Defence called Colonel Indic who said: "As far as I know, General Galic never met with the Egyptian battalion commander. He was the only battalion commander that he didn't meet with because he never requested such a meeting." That had not been put to General Abdel Razek by the Defence when he gave his evidence. Mr. President, the next image that will appear on the screen is another map that was tendered through Dr. Radinovic. The Defence has not clearly articulated the use that it thinks the Trial Chamber should make of this map beyond stating that it demonstrates the potential for collateral damage and the difficulty posed to the accused in protecting the civilian population on the Bosnian government side of the confrontation lines. That's in their written submissions at paragraph 793. I make these observations about the map: It transpires that there are 225 targets marked on it. 70 of those, or 30 per cent approximately, are in the Stup, Halilovici, Alipasin Most area, which appears as a large clump on the left-hand side or the west of the city. Indeed, one might think looking at it broadly speaking, there are two major clumps. The bigger of those to is the one to the left, being to the west. But that of course is what you would expect given that it is not the main residential part of the city. None of the scheduled sniping or shelling incidents occurred in that part of the city. You may recall, Mr. President and Your Honours, seeing a photograph taken from the site of sniping incident 16 and 17, looking southwest across the western plains of the city, the railway yards, an industrial area predominantly. So there is nothing irresponsible about that aspect of the pattern. The second largest grouping is in the centre of the city where we have, we heard, the Marsal Tito barracks, a military barracks. But more importantly, it is also the area where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps under the command of the accused made its final attempt to divide the city. We heard that occurred in October 1992, Milada Halili who lived in the square told us in that month there was an attack by the SRK sources. Mr. Tucker also told us that that was the last attempt by the SRK to militarily resolve the armed conflict. It therefore makes perfect sense that there would be of necessity some defence assets in that critical area. It happens to be, as we have heard, immediately to the left of it and to the right of it, two areas of intense civilian residences. A further point I make is that on closer examination of the documents which are set -- which are said by the Defence to found this map, many of the references indicate that the positions existed only in the pre-indictment period. They have no reference to existing in the indictment period. Examination will also reveal that many of the numbers are duplicates. In other words, there is more than one number referring to the same object or position. The next image on the screen will demonstrate most of those entries which are either pre-indictment or duplicated. They are now indicated in white. That has been added by the Prosecution. It is not complete. They are not all of the duplications and pre-indictment positions, but they are many of them. A third point --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression that this map which was examined by the Prosecution wasn't submitted during the investigations, and we don't think that this is an appropriate step to take. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map has not been presented during the investigations. I do not...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please respond, Mr. Ierace. The next map the Defence feels has not been shown before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It is not obviously the intention of the Prosecution to tender it. This is a visual way of economically making a point through submissions. The parties and the Trial Chamber itself can examine at its leisure the documents, those which can be identified at least, as the basis for the map. And on so doing, I anticipate the Trial Chamber will discover the point that I have made. Mr. President, I infer from what my learned colleague has said that he contends that there is something inappropriate about the use of such a visual aid. And that I would respectfully dispute, that this is a proper mechanism to make the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the use of the map is limited to visually assisting the Chamber in what you are presenting to the Chamber as your argument, you're allowed to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is the case, Mr. President. Excuse me for a moment. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, again on this map, we see the airport, the runway about which I have made some comments. Over the next short while, I will make some observations in relation to the evidence moving in an anti-clockwise direction around the city. Moving firstly to Dobrinja, then to the areas adjacent -- immediately adjacent to Nedzarici, then to Alipasino Polje. And in that same fashion, move eastwards along the southern half of the city area, then around to the northeast, into Kobila Glava, and then to of course to Rajlovac. In so doing, I do not intend to repeat what is in the oral submissions, but instead to draw together different aspects of the evidence. That will come increasingly evident when we come to the area of Grbavci. Mr. President, we will now go to the next image, which is a detail of the map of Dr. Radinovic of the area of Dobrinja, and one sees on that detail one of the white circles marked by the Prosecution being number 82. So this is a map offered by the Defence identifying military targets within Dobrinja. Mr. President, perhaps I should at this stage make this point as well. We have heard reference in questions put by the Defence to various witnesses to the notion of legitimate military targets, witnesses have been asked whether various buildings, various facilities were legitimate military targets. I don't know that that term has any generally understood currency in international humanitarian law, but if it is to be used, it seems to the Prosecution that one must distinguish between a military target and a legitimate military target. To give a simple example, a sniper operating in a field is a military target. A sniper operating on a hospital ward is a military target. The distinction between them is that the sniper in the hospital ward in particular, depending on the proposed method of neutralising that sniper, may well not be a legitimate military target. So on this map, we see what is offered as military targets. The first observation I make is that you will note that there are three circles with number 47. And again, to illustrate the incompleteness of the use of white on the circles, none of these have been marked white. The document which purports to found the reference to 47 refers -- is a directive in relation to the 5th Motorised Brigade of the ABiH, a directive in relation to general lines of defence. In other words, to be more accurately positioned, number 47 should have been at the confrontation lines, not in the centre of Dobrinja or away from the confrontation lines. It will soon become apparent that the middle circle with 47 is in the vicinity -- has been placed in the vicinity of sniper incident number 18. But on the basis of the document, it shouldn't be there. It should be either to the left or to the right on the front lines. Number 99, according to the documents tendered, refers to a particular document which the Prosecution is unable to locate. It refers to an order made on the 15th. The order is described as 15/93. We have seen order 14/93, but not 15/93. But in any event, it appears that it is not an SRK document -- I'm sorry. In any event, it is not an ABiH document, it is an SRK document. And therefore, one might think is based ultimately on SRK intelligence. We are therefore left with this dilemma: What does do with the reference to 99 where there is no document; and even if there was, it seems it's an SRK intelligence document? What is the basis of the positioning? Number 75 is a timetable for the regulation of traffic through the tunnel under the airport. There's no clear indication as to why 75 is placed in this location. 52, which is beneath it, is accurately placed as being where the tunnel is. And I note from the evidence, if that is placed there as being relevant to the second shelling incident, that we've heard that the tunnel began to operate after that incident occurred, on the 12th of July, 1993. So the point I make is that it's necessary to look very carefully at the foundational -- the foundation of these circles, of these entries, in order to determine whether any sensible use can be made of them. And finally, I come to circle 118, which happens to be placed squarely on the position of the first scheduled shelling incident. The document we could not locate. What we can determine from the other documentation is that apparently it's based on an SRK intelligence report. In any event, the document is apparently dated the 31st of January, 1994, being well after the date of the first shelling incident. I go now to the next image. And here we see the tendered Prosecution map, tendered by the Prosecution, indicating the positions where the victims of sniping incidents 6, 18, and 22 were located. We've heard evidence that there was a church of the orthodox faith partly constructed at the commencement of the war, remained in that state throughout the war, and was located in the area where we see the red circle to the right of the screen. One can note from this map, having regard to the light-blue line that cuts moving from right to left diagonally to the enter of the map and then levels out to a horizontal centre line, that being the Dobrinja River. But from the position of the church, one had a vantage point down a considerable length of the river, in particular, incorporating positions 6 and 18. On this map also, we see the confrontation lines as evidenced by General Karavelic, the commander of the ABiH, the modification made by him with a dark-blue line made to the left. SRK forward positions dark green, ABiH forward positions a lighter green. Sniping incident 6 occurred on the 11th of July, 1993. It involved a group of civilians who relied upon the water of the river which really at that point was a cement-lined canal as their source of water for washing, it being not sufficiently clean for drinking. But that, they went to a water point elsewhere in Dobrinja which happens to be the site of the first shelling incident, scheduled shelling incident, where, according to in relation to incident 6, the deceased victim's 16 year old daughter, 16 years at the time, they would sometimes wait 10 to 12 hours to fill their plastic containers with drinking water. That first scheduled shelling incident occurred the day after this sniping incident. The -- we heard from a friend and neighbour of the deceased victim, the victim being a 48-year-old woman dressed on that day in a skirt, that the two went to a small bridge across the river that joined the different parts of Dobrinja. When they arrived, they noticed that civilians before them were taking shelter against the side of the bridge so that they were sheltered from the east. That is, the same direction in which there was the church. They could see bullets hitting the water surface alongside them. After a while, the shooting stopped. And one civilian, and then another in turn, proceeded to the water's edge and filled their containers and retreated. The third civilian to attempt that manoeuvre was the victim. And when she arrived at the water's edge, she was shot. She turned, and she was shot again. And she fell back into the water. The witness, her friend, who gave evidence, said that she moved to retrieve her friend, the victim, but was stopped by other civilians because the shooting continued. It continued for some time, bullets hitting the water. Eventually, a group of soldiers emerged, took up positions on the bridge, and returned fire to the church, to the direction of the church. And ultimately, by the use of a rope or a belt or something of that order, the victim was retrieved. The Defence in its written submissions portrays a different picture, and one for which there is absolutely no evidence. The Defence portrayal is that the soldiers were firing from the bridge at the time that the victim was shot. They suggest that -- the Defence suggests that while fire was being exchanged from the bridge to the SRK positions, this group of civilians, middle-aged women amongst them, were content to, beneath that same bridge, collect water. All the evidence is one way. The soldiers arrived after the victim was shot. The Defence next suggests that there was no line of sight between the church and where the victim was shot. Or to put it another way, it was not possible from the church to see where the woman was shot. The Defence called evidence to the effect that the church had been shelled. The dome of the church had been hit, the inference was that it was so damaged that you could not accommodate snipers in that church. That witness was confronted by the Prosecution with photographs taken at the end of the war, and he agreed that those photographs portrayed precisely the condition of the church during the war, during the indictment period. Those photographs will appear on the screen shortly. That is one on the screen now. And I should say, Mr. President, that we have placed the exhibit numbers of these photographs electronically on the screen. We see the church in the centre of the photograph, and alongside it, a building crane. The witness said the building crane was there throughout the war as well. We note on the maps, such as the sniping maps, such as the one we saw earlier, that alongside the circle is the word "tower" or "towers," an apparent reference to the building condition of the site as it was before the war. The next image is a different view, a close-up view of the church, and we see at the top of the tower a large opening and we see also scaffolding around it. Witnesses gave evidence that there was scaffolding around the church throughout the war. The Prosecution submits that we are looking at an ideal position in which to place a sniper or snipers. It is a structure which has a commanding view of the surrounding terrain. It is a structure which is softened by the scaffolding and has a number of openings within it which could be used for that purpose. The next image, which we now see, shows the tower from a different angle. And to be clear on this, the Defence witness agreed that that opening on the tower is the way it was during the war. Having regard to the edges of that opening, there is certainly no visual evidence of a shelling, and there is nothing about the appearance of the church in the three photographs that detracts from its use as a source of sniping. The next image, we heard evidence, was taken from precisely where the victim was shot. Tendered into evidence was the statement of Zoran Lesic, who took a series of photographs and videos together with his assistants of the various scheduled sniping incidents. We saw the witness, the friend of the victim, on the video at the bridge indicating where the victim was positioned at the time she was shot. We saw a yellow cross placed on that position with yellow paint on the cement. The statement of Mr. Lesic is to the effect that he would erect his tripod directly over those yellow markings, place the camera at an approximate height as to that of which the bullet entered the body, and then take electronically 360 degree photographs. So we are able to see on this photograph what lines of sight there were from where the victim was shot. This is evidence that can't be contested that the church was able to be seen, and therefore, there was a line of sight from the church. It appears white in this photograph because it was taken we've heard in the last few years in which time the building has been completed and it has been painted. The witness circled the church. We move on to the next image which is a map marked by investigator Kucanin. We see Dobrinja to the left, and where we see a G, it looks a little like a 6, is where he placed the church. And it was known he said as the Veljine church in Dobrinja. To the right, in the vicinity of the O marked in blue, he indicated Lukavica barracks. We see just left to the O some dark silhouettes which correspond to the building complex. We heard evidence that those were the accused's forward headquarters - his main headquarters apparently being in Pale - his forward headquarters for this conflict. One notes, having regard to the map, the distance between the accused's headquarters and the church and in turn, Dobrinja, and the airport. To the bottom left corner of the map, one can make out the lines of the runway. Next image is indeed some video. This video which we're about to see, which we're now seeing, was tendered by the Defence through one of its witnesses. The white building was the headquarters for the accused. He was on the top floor, on this same corner area of the building. If we could pause at this point. We see Mojmilo hill, we just Mojmilo hill on the screen. Excuse me, Mr. President. We're not able to pause it for the moment. So in a few minutes, between the trees, one will see the church as it could be seen from this area. And the witness identified it as being the same church, Veljine. It will appear on the screen to the left of Mojmilo hill in between the trucks. It appears there now just between the leafs, that high structure. Now, the Defence witness went on to say that there were barricades erected suggesting perhaps that the church couldn't be seen from the building, but that is not the point. The point is not whether the accused would have heard the firing by the snipers. The point is that given the evidence as to the command and control which the accused enjoyed over his subordinates, it is unthinkable that a sniping -- snipers could operate from that church so physically close to his headquarters without it being sanctioned by him. That is the point. Not the line of sight, but the physical proximity. The same can be said of the mortar units the Prosecution says were responsible for the mortaring of the football game and the humanitarian gathering in Dobrinja. The evidence is that those units came from approximately that area, the area adjacent to the Lukavica headquarters. Is it credible that individuals could have operated mortars so close to the accused's headquarters without him sanctioning that behaviour? We move now to incident 18 in some more detail. The next image. We see a sniping map relative to that incident. No different than the earlier. We move on to the next image. And this incident, very briefly, involved a 32-year-old woman who was riding her bicycle across the next bridge along from where the previous incident occurred, that is, the next bridge to the east, closer to the church, closer to the front lines. As she rode her bicycle on the 6th of January, 1994, she noticed bullets impacting on the road around her, and then realised she had been shot in the buttocks. The witness marked a photograph and participated in a video, a 360-degree photograph was taken. We now move on to the next image. We have a problem, Mr. President, of a technical nature, I think. Rather than come back to this piece of footage, it's only a matter of seconds, but it's a problem which is going to recur, I wonder if we could have a very short adjournment to see if we can correct it. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any time how much time it would take, Mr. Ierace? Because the Chamber has considered that after one hour, we could have a longer break, and that would give you more time to make repairs. Otherwise, we might risk that we have to make short breaks again and again, which would take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, it may be that we cannot obtain any assistance until 10.30. That being the case, I won't show this videoclip. I'll move on. Excuse me. So I'll move on, Mr. President, at least until the next videoclip, and then perhaps suggest a change. So we could move now to the next image, we see a photograph marked by this witness looking east from the northern end of the bridge. She marked with the dark crosshatching a barricade that existed at the time. She circled the church, and she also indicated, and one can appreciate this by comparing photograph to the map, that there were apartment buildings which also were under the control of the SRK and from which there was a line of sight to her. She gave evidence that following this incident, the barricades were extended and changed to sandbags from a less substantial nature. We move on now to the next incident, incident 22, where the victims were in Dobrinja, the firing, Prosecution says, emanating from the other side of the confrontation line, that is, to the west, territory of Nedzarici, held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And a brief reminder of the evidence about this: On the 25th of May, 1994, during a cease-fire, a bus pulled up at its last stop at the end of the run, position being 22, that red dot. The bus driver gave evidence that he heard a single shot coming from the direction of Nedzarici, that is, from the west. The bullet hit the bus, impacted ultimately on two middle-aged women who were passengers on the bus. Indeed, one of the women suffered a laceration to an artery. He restarted the bus and drove straight to the nearby hospital, the Dobrinja hospital. If we move to the next image, this was marked by the witness. This is the road that we earlier saw on the map looking to the west. That is where he heard the shot come from. And on the next image, we see another photograph marked by him showing with red crosshatching where there was a barricade at the time, and also two dwellings which either didn't exist at the time or were in a state of partial construction. The Defence contends that the distance involved between the site of this incident and the building known as the school of theology in Nedzarici was so great that it could not have been the source of fire. The Defence also suggested in evidence it called that the lay of the land, the nature of the terrain between the school of theology and the confrontation lines did not allow for the possibility that the shooter could have been located on that territory. The bus driver gave evidence that he could see the school of theology from where the bus was hit. And having regard to the state of these buildings at the time that we see on the photograph, there was terrain in between the school of theology and the confrontation lines from where the round could have emanated. The Prosecution does not suggest with any certainty a particular place on that territory as to where the bullet came from, nor, in our respectful submission, is that a prerequisite to proving these charges. Mr. President, at this juncture, may I also make this observation, earlier I noted that at this stage of the trial, it is of course open to the Trial Chamber to apply in a proper fashion findings of fact from one body of evidence to other issues in the trial. In its written submissions, the Defence repeatedly suggested that these various sniping incidents were not made out because there was no identification with precision of who fired and precisely where from. And if these were individual trials, each of these scheduled sniping incidents, in which the evidence, the only Prosecution evidence, was that offered in relation to each sniping incident, it would more often than not be the case that we could not prove them. But that is an unrealistic view of the evidence in this trial. This evidence is to be combined with other evidence, evidence of admissions by the accused and his subordinates and so on, evidence of admissions, together with evidence of observations made by a number of witnesses as to what lay on the other side, evidence of observations of a number of witnesses as to the behaviour of the SRK soldiers, snipers, professional snipers, at least full-time snipers on the SRK side. It is unaccountably unrealistic in our respectful submission for the Defence to confine itself hermetically to the evidence of each scheduled incident in a discrete fashion. And so, in this case, for instance, there is evidence from a number of sources that the school of theology was regarded by civilians at the time and investigators as a source of sniping fire. This gives rise to a second issue. A number of witnesses, civilians, war correspondents, medical people, as well military observers have given evidence of observing the source of fire. Sometimes that evidence has been in the form of observing tracer rounds or smoke or light of some form emanating from a barrel. For example, in relation to scheduled sniping incident 16 and 17, the building on the plain to the southwest was where one of the witnesses we heard saw light at night, at dusk, flashes of light, when persons in that building shot from it. There is nothing in our respectful submission that detracts from full weight to be given to such evidence. Evidence of that nature does not require any special skill. Sometimes that evidence goes a step further and is to the effect that fire came from the SRK side of the confrontation lines. And of course, if we're talking of rounds that could be seen, tracer rounds and so on, it follows that the source of those rounds, depending on what view one has, can also be determined in a simple and reliable fashion. We have heard evidence that the barricades that were set up around Sarajevo increasingly set up from late 1992 onwards were effective. In other words, when civilians used them, the risk that they were shot from the SRK side of the confrontation lines was reduced. The number of casualties as a result dropped. We heard evidence from one of the local witnesses, the head of civil defence, that after the war when the barricades were taken down, he carefully inspected them, and he found that the impacts were on the SRK side, that is, the side facing the SRK front lines. Sometimes bullets would penetrate those membranes, even steel membranes, even containers. That is powerful relevant evidence as to where the fire came from which targeted civilians. The fact that the barricades worked. Returning to this incident and the images, at this point, we can move on, except I think we have another video. We'll leave that and move -- excuse me, Mr. President. We'll move on. We come now to the areas adjacent to Nedzarici. Dobrinja is to the bottom right. We see the SRK-held territory in the form of a salient into ABiH territory. And again, we see some white circles, pre-indictment positions, or repeats. We see again number 47 -- withdraw that. We see 47 with a blue colouring. And again, that is a directive on general lines of defence. We have seen number 47 three times in the Dobrinja map. And if you, Mr. President and Your Honours, consult the bigger version, you will see immediately above the 138 yet again 47. The numbers to the right, 84 and 164, on the basis of the documents that found them, refer to the Mojmilo neighbourhood. In other words, there is no particular apparent reason as to why they have been placed in that precise position. If one looks at the scale of this may it please, one can deduce that the diameter of these circles is some 200 metres. And yet, the target may be something much smaller than that, a room, a small building. When one looks at the map as a whole, that has been to be taken into account, that while in some areas, the circles appear to all but cover the ground, that is in part because the diameter chosen by the individual or individuals who constructed this map. If, and this hasn't been made clear by the Defence, if the suggestion is that 200 metres is deliberately chosen so as to indicate an acceptable area of targeting for a building, the Prosecution submits strongly against that. It is inappropriate, in the Prosecution's submission, to utilise in a densely populated, urban setting weaponry that is so indiscriminate by its nature, quite separate from those who operate it. We heard evidence in the Defence case, and indeed, from some Prosecution witnesses, that one does not expect in normal circumstances to hit the target on the first shell. Mr. Stamp will talk more about that at a later point. But that is a factor to be taken into account by those who make the decisions. If that is their expectation, that the target will not be hit by the first shell, then the mortar is in many circumstances in an urban setting inappropriate as a weapon to use. Perhaps we'll move on to the next image now. We see now the sniping map for incident 13. That was the independent where a 15-year-old boy, the indictment said 16, it transpired he was 15, did not go to school on the 4th of October, 1993, ironically because his mother was concerned for his safety. A civilian had been shot that morning. So instead, he accompanied his father, who was making a delivery on behalf of the civil defence authorities of foodstuff or water to a civilian settlement. They proceeded along the main road, which appears on this image, on the top third of the image. Marsal Tito Boulevard, turned left, they proceeded from left to right as one looks at the map, turned left in Ante Babica Street, where we see the two white shed buildings to the left of the intersection, they being student hostels. The truck had a heavy load. The father and the son gave evidence, and that evidence was to the effect that the truck proceeded slowly after the intersection. It is a slope. The driver said he was travelling at about 20 or 30 kilometres per hour. He said that the student hostels were hollow, the floors were hollow. Not surprising, one would think, given the Defence evidence that the buildings had been used by ABiH forces. On the map, we see the position of the buildings known as the school or home for the blind circled close to the confrontation lines. The driver said that he had driven this road many times before, and he had been shot at before from the vicinity of the school for the blind. As he approached the intersection, he noticed a barricade had been erected 2 metres high, concrete blocks. The evidence from the father or the son was that the barricade in fact had been erected that day. There was an UNPROFOR APC parked just beyond the intersection. His truck was 3 metres high; the barricades were 2 metres high. It was marked as a butcher's truck, his vocation. His son was in the passenger seat closest to the SRK side. On the video, by comparing the video with a photograph that he marked, which I'll show shortly, it's apparent that when the truck was hit by the bullet, it had passed the barricades. There was a line of sight even putting to one side the height evidence. The Prosecution makes these observations. The relevance of the student hostels having hollow floors is not that persons were necessarily shot through those floors, but rather, persons on the SRK territory had the opportunity to see vehicles and individuals who they wished to target approach the intersection. They had time to prepare, time to raise their rifles, to take aim, to watch. On this particular occasion, not only could the truck have been seen approaching the intersection through the student hostel, but also above the 2-metre barricades so that they end at a steadily slow speed, ideal conditions for a sniper to anticipate and shoot, which is what happened, and the 15-year-old was shot. The Defence suggests that a cloud hangs over the status of the father as to whether he was a combatant. Assuming hypothetically that he was a combatant, that does not relieve the accused or his subordinates. The Prosecution submits that it is inappropriate in those circumstances to shoot at a combatant when there is a child in the way. But more to the point, what was there about them which suggested that he was a combatant? They were wearing civilian clothes, a civilian-marked truck. There was nothing. In any event, he was working for civil defence. Mr. President, there is someone here now who can attend to the technical problem. I wonder if we could take the break perhaps 10 minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. I have difficulties looking at the clock because it's reflecting, but it's close to 25 minutes past 10.00, as far as I can see. We'll resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I was informed that it was a network problem rather than anything that would have been done wrong in the preparation. So therefore, I hope that everything functions now well. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the break, I was referring to incident -- scheduled sniping incident number 1. The driver of the truck, the father of the victim, gave evidence that from where his son was shot, it was possible to see the home for the blind, and indeed, he had seen a hole on the first floor of that building which afforded visibility to the intersection. Mr. President, the Prosecution case featured much evidence about that particular facility. The Defence called a number of what one might call front-line troops who served for the SRK in Nedzarici, and many of them came tantalisingly close to saying that they were stationed in the home for the blind, but ultimately, none of them ever did. The Defence case was that the home was not utilised as a source of sniping fire. Reason: That it was too dangerous to leave the ground floor and go into the upper floors. That was an explanation which the Prosecution submits lacks credibility. The Defence witnesses said that they were subject to fire from the high-rise buildings surrounding Nedzarici. Implicit in that evidence was an appreciation of the strategic importance of high elevation points, positions which afforded a view over the enemy positions. They in Nedzarici had view buildings to utilise in that fashion. The home for the blind, a matter of a few floors; the school of theology, significantly more floors. And yet, they departed from their strategic observations to deny that those buildings were so used. Indeed, the Defence case is a little difficult to understand in relation to whether the SRK had snipers, sniper units, or sniper rifles. In their written submissions at paragraph 11, the Defence stated its position to be that the SRK had no sniper weapons. At paragraph 508, it said the SRK did have sniper weapons, but no snipers. Dr. Radinovic said they had snipers. Based on his conversations with various officers of the SRK. A number of witnesses gave evidence of seeing sniper weapons in the SRK. A Defence witness gave evidence of seeing one in the headquarters of the accused. The ultimate conclusion we would submit is that the SRK had sniper weapons and snipers. Those sniper weapons were M76 rifles, the Russian version being known as the Draganov, equipped with a long barrel and an optical sight, capable of shooting single rounds, according to the literature, with accuracy to 1.000 metres. According to some witnesses, capable of accurate use beyond 1.000 metres. The distance involved in relation to Nedzarici was much less than that. In the vicinity of 450 metres. One didn't necessarily need a professional sniper rifle to send off a burst of lethal rounds from Nedzarici to civilians who were passing close to the front line. Coming back to incident number 13, we should see on the screen shortly a photograph that was marked by a witness to another incident at that site. We see the student hostel to the right, high-rise buildings to the left. And in the middle, a building which I think was three storeys, but in a depression, so the ground level was beneath the road level. The witness, Mr. Kapetanovic, crosshatched the roof. He recollected that that building didn't have a roof. The father of the victim in this incident recollected that that building wasn't even -- that building had two floors at that stage. In any event, his evidence is that you could see the home for the blind. Mr. President, I make this further general observation: That there is a tendency to become too technical and too detailed, to examine too minutely the evidence in relation to many of these scheduled sniping incidents. The Defence in its submissions, on more than one occasion, has sought to rely on discrepancies between the evidence of victims and witnesses in order to undermine the credibility of the witnesses. There is nothing wrong with that in theory. That is an accepted technique of testing the credibility of a witness. By the same token, differences do not mean that the credibility is undermined. It's a matter of human nature and common sense to conclude that of course people have varying degrees of recall, especially after ten years. And that when incidents happen quickly, even if they're spoken to straight afterwards, there will be differences which don't reflect on their credibility as a whole. These incidents which occurred adjacent to the home for the blind are typical in that regard. There can be no doubt in my respectful submission, that the victims of these incidents were clearly shot from the SRK side and were targeted. And that is as far as the Prosecution seeks to go with them. The Prosecution relies on other evidence to connect the accused as the commander of those troops in a 7(1) capacity. I invite -- I respectfully invite the Trial Chamber to imagine on the basis of the evidence, and only the evidence, of course, what happened. The truck moved up the street. There was one shot as it slowly drove past the intersection, it impacted on the frame of the passenger door, the bullet fragmented and hit the son in the neck. And that's it. Simple occurrence of events leading, as an exercise of common sense, to a simple conclusion. One shot in those circumstances is deliberate. The people in that front seat were targeted. I move on to the next image, and here we see a marking made by the victim's father of the barricade which existed on that intersection on that day. I draw your attention to the length of the barricade. It was a very small barricade. The evidence is that it later was extended. He gave some evidence about the length of trees, the height of trees I should say, at the time, drew lines to indicate what the height was at the time. Next image, please. You will recollect much controversy with Defence witnesses as to where this photograph was taken from. The Defence -- the Prosecution submitted it was taken from the top level of one of the buildings of the home for the blind complex immediately adjacent to the street that we see -- either section that we see in the photograph. One Defence witness in spite of the appearance of the drainpipe suggests that it couldn't have been taken from that building, even though he later acknowledged that the drainpipe was part of that building. He resisted as long as he could that suggestion, but ultimately relented. He had maintained that you couldn't see the intersection from the home for the blind. This photograph demonstrates that you could. The next photograph is a telephoto shot of the section we see above the red roof to the left. One sees a line of sight. The Defence said, oh, yes, but there were a series of barricades leading up to the intersection which blocked the view. When confronted with this photograph, that particular Defence witness agreed that you could see over at least the first two rows of barricades to the intersection, but said, of course, they never went to the upper storeys of the home for the blind. This photograph also makes clear that the position where the victim was shot, keeping in mind the position of the barricade, was east -- rather south, I should say, of that position. In other words, the barricade did not at all impede the line of sight. Rather than go back to the relevant piece of video, you may remember, Mr. President and Your Honours, that the position was to the right of the intersection, slightly to the right. Next image, please. And next one. This is a photograph taken by a reserve policeman who witnessed the shooting of the victims of sniping incident 21. A 63-year-old man, a pensioner, was walking with a 57-year-old friend and another man of senior years along Ante Babica Street, which is the street running along the bottom of the photograph from right to left. The reserve policeman was in the vicinity, heard two shots, at first thought he was the target, and he was in the direction of the blue arrow that we see at the bottom of the photograph, according to his evidence, although that was not the reason that arrow was placed on the photograph. He gave evidence that gauging on the sound of the shots, they came from the direction of the school for the blind. He investigated and located the injured parties, assisted to the best that he could. One of the victims died two and a half months later as a result of his injuries. The third person who wasn't injured gave evidence. At the time he gave evidence, he was aged 71 and in poor health to the extent that he had to testify by videolink from Sarajevo. Clearly, he was confused with respect to some of the photographs. The Defence, in its written submissions, relies heavily on discrepancies between his evidence and that of the reserve policeman. But again, I submit it's appropriate to step back and take a common sense view. Firstly, is it seriously suggested that the two men were not shot, that they were not shot in that general area? The evidence of the reserve policeman was very credible and in turn, logical and simple. He heard the shots. He was able to indicate where they came from, and he found the victims, and he attended them. Again, keeping in mind what the Prosecution sets out to prove, simply that persons were targeted, they were civilians, and they were shot from the SRK side, that is done beyond reasonable doubt. The reserve policeman noted that it was a cease-fire on that day, and he said of cease-fires: "The population behaved in a more relaxed manner. They could move freely, and they could move more. When the cease-fire was on, our task was often especially on areas exposed to the sniper fire. We would be given a task to warn those people because the cease-fire often meant nothing. When there were not cease-fires, people, especially women and children, spent their time in cellars." Now, the Defence has also said in its submissions that the sniping scheduled incidents occurred close to the front line in a combat zone. And I use this one -- or these incidents involving the home for the blind as an example to respond to this Defence submission. The Defence points out that persons were not sniped well away from the front line. Well, that is hardly surprising given the range of professional sniper weapons. They have to be, if that is the weapon used, within that distance of where the shooter is located. The Prosecution case is that the accused deployed not only professional sniper weapons, but bursts of fire from infantry weapons, assault rifles, machine-guns, anti-aircraft artillery, and that extended the range of such weapons well into the city. But this notion that the Defence proposes of a combat zone warrants closer examination. What exactly is the Defence proposing? That there were agreed combat zones from which civilians were excluded? There is no evidentiary basis for that at all. The Defence has suggested time and again it was incumbent upon the Bosnian government authorities to move civilians out of Sarajevo, out of harm's way. I pose the rhetorical question: "Where to"? A city of 340.000 people, the biggest city in Bosnia, where were they to move to? Which state? Which international agency was offering accommodation for that number of people and the support mechanisms they needed? The Prosecution [sic] suggests: "Well, they should have been moved at least away from areas immediately adjacent to the front lines." But as this photograph indicates, taken from the top of one of the residential complexes on the Bosnian government side, and as the earlier photographs indicate -- demonstrate even more dramatically, it happened that the structures which offered bulk accommodation to the residents of Sarajevo were close to the front line. If the high-rises of Alipasino Polje, those many blocks of 20 storeys, were to be emptied, where in the city, leaving to one side out of the city, were those residents, those civilian residents, to be accommodated? In the old city? On open land in the Sedrenik area? Perhaps in the industrial area. There is and was no alternative. Milada Halili explained that she and her husband and her mother lived very close to the front line in Heroes' square in Hrasno. Her mother became deeply concerned for her own safety following the 1992 assault by SRK forces. So she moved to the PTT building where the evidence was she lived in that building. It didn't save her because ultimately, she had to emerge from the building, and she had to make her way around the city. And as we'll shortly see, and we've heard the evidence, she was shot dead. It is a little insincere, inconsistent certainly, for the Defence to make this proposition in any event given that its own witnesses operating on the SRK admitted that there were civilians living close to the front lines on their side. Nedzarici was a very small area, in the order of a kilometre across. There were hundreds of civilians living in Nedzarici. One defence soldier said his mother lived there within 200 metres of the front line. He explained she didn't want to move, and so she continued to live there. He was asked whether he expected that on the other side of the line a similar situation would apply. And he thought not. Defence witness after Defence witness said the same thing. That they were not informed there were civilians living so close. This aspect of the evidence is a convenient point to deal with another issue raised by the Defence. And that is, who precisely in the Defence case was targeted? Witnesses who were SRK troops in Nedzarici said that they regularly received orders not to target civilians once a week, at least. One wonders why there was a need for such orders if they weren't targeting civilians? There is an internal inconsistency in that evidence. When asked what that meant, they said that it meant not to target children, not to target women, not to target anyone who was not wearing a uniform. Some went so far as to say they were not to target uniformed adults, men, unless they were armed and threatening them. So there is between this evidence and the Prosecution evidence an enormous gulf. It seems the Defence case is that no SRK soldiers ever targeted women or persons in civilian clothes. How could it be, then, that thousands were injured as a result of shooting or shelling? No explanation is offered for that. There is indeed another inconsistency in the Defence case. While that is the effect of its evidence, its submissions are different. In its submissions, it enthusiastically submits that there was nothing wrong with targeting a woman because she might be a soldier, especially if she was in the combat zone. The written submissions observe that a 7-year-old could be used for military purposes. There is no explanation offered as to the gulf between the submissions and the Defence evidence. What is the Defence position? More importantly, how can they make submissions not based on the evidence? That nexus must always apply. Submissions should never venture into the hypothetical. They should never be fantastical. They should reflect the evidence. I move on to the next image.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We see here Mr. Kapetanovic being asked certain questions by an investigator. And this was one of the benefits of the videoevidence, because whatever difficulties civilian witnesses had in relating to maps and photographs, this was an opportunity for them to orientate themselves at the actual site where the incidents occurred. Mr. Kapetanovic, the third man, the one who wasn't shot, is indicating on this video the direction in which he and his companions were walking as he remembers it. And more importantly, the position where the shooting happened. We see in the background on the right the student hostel, evidence being that the floors were hollow. We see in the middle the red-roofed building. Mr. Kapetanovic's evidence that the roof wasn't there. The evidence of the investigator that the building wasn't there -- I'm sorry, the reserve policeman, I should say. And there is seen to be no inconsistency between Mr. Kapetanovic's evidence and that of the reserve policeman, that them being shot from the school for the blind was possible. That there was a line of sight when one factors in the situation with the red-roofed building. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. We move on now to the next image, and this is incident number 23. That is the sniping map. Very briefly, a couple walked up the street we see to the right at the dot. And as they did say, the woman was shot in her hand. The shooting continued. They took cover on the ground. The Prosecution case is that the round came from the vicinity of the cone that we see on the map, to the west of the front-line positions. The victim gave evidence -- indeed both gave evidence that the sound associated with the shooting, the sound of the shooting, came from that direction. Can we please go to the next image. Here we see the couple at the place where they were shot. The victim's brother-in-law alongside her facing west. Nedzarici in the background. The next shot is a telephoto from the same position. In the background, we see a white flat-roofed building behind the lamppost on the right. The victim circled that building, indicating it to be the school of theology. There was -- keeping in mind that the houses between the school of theology and the street behind the couple involves post-war construction, the Prosecution is not able to say with any certainty beyond the front line where that shot came from. But given the shooting continued, there is evidence they were targeted. They were civilians, and she was dressed in a skirt or dress on the day. There was nothing about them, in other words, to suggest otherwise than they were civilians. Next photograph, next image. Incident 25. A girl aged 16 years with her girlfriend, a year younger, were crossing a road. The 16-year-old was shot in the shoulder. They were making their way back to the friend's apartment. The friend gave evidence. Some ABiH soldiers called out to them to take care because there was some shooting. They ran across the street as a result of that warning. They were told that sniper fire had started up. The girls were wearing civilian clothes, jeans, T-shirt, sneakers. We have some video of the witness explaining where the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the interests of saving time, we won't play the rest of the video, but the witness has now indicated where they crossed the road and shortly after this point, she indicated where the victim was shot, which was immediately in front of her. If we continue a little bit, I'll tell you when to pause. All right, that will do. We'll go to the next one. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 21709 to 21722. We will shortly see a 360-degree photograph taken from the site where the victim was shot. And we have a problem, so I will move on. The 360-degree photograph panning the area from that site indicated as we saw on the video Nedzarici in the background, and the school for the blind clearly visible. This photograph taken from the same position as the earlier photograph from the school for the blind, but in a different direction. That can be deduced by comparing this photograph with the one taken in the direction of Ante Babica Street. It ad joins to the left of this photograph. The next image shows a gap which appears between the buildings. Thank you. And we see a building which was not there at the time crosshatched by the witness, and to the right, the place where the victim was shot. Next image. And we now move on to incident 26. In the same vicinity as 25, and one can see from the map that there was a gap in the buildings slightly to the west of where the victim was when he was shot. Next image, please. We see that gap in the centre of the photograph. The victim was on one of the upper floors of the building immediately behind. Having regard to the map, it's clear this photograph was taken from SRK-held territory. Next photograph. We see here the building in which the victim was at the time, where he lived, and we note the damage done to that sliver of the wall of buildings, consistent with the gap that we saw in the earlier photograph. In other words, these buildings received considerable fire during the war, not necessarily, therefore, the indictment period, or exclusively the indictment period, as a result of fire from the west. No evidence as to when that damage was caused. Next image. The victim is here seen seated where he was when shot. We note the balcony behind him. Next image. The close-up of that balcony reveals in the background the area which by comparison with the map is where the front line was. And although it doesn't appear clearly in this particular photograph, we are able to see the institute of theology, the school of theology, above the red roofs. That was identified in evidence. Thank you. Next one. And then we move on to the next image. Before we do, the evidence in relation to incident 26 is that there was coverings over the glass. The question then becomes: What is the Prosecution case? If he could not be seen as an individual, what does the Prosecution submit happened? He and his family were watching TV, television. There was a light source. The Prosecution submits that the targeting was no more than that, hitting a light source. That is indiscriminate fire. It doesn't matter that the person who fired the rifle, the weapon, could not see the victim. What is relevant is whether the shooter knowingly fired indiscriminately, unaware as to who, if anyone, was behind the glass area covered and their identity, and their status, most significantly. The Prosecution case, as articulated in the pre-trial brief and our written submissions, has consistently been that civilians were targeted either deliberately or indiscriminately. And this is an example of indiscriminate shooting. The evidence is that the SRK not only had sniper weapons and optical sights fitted to sniper weapons, and indeed, machine guns, but also devices allowing them to shoot at night, that is, night sights. And whatever light emanated from that apartment area would be far more apparent with night sight devices which the SRK had. Move on to the image on the screen at the moment. This is a map marked by John Ashton who initially went to Sarajevo as a journalist, later worked for UNHCR, and after that set up an agency with others who provided material assistance to doctors and hospitals operating on both sides of the confrontation line. With his journalist background, Mr. Ashton was very handy with a camera. And that made him a particularly interesting witness in being able to offer some images of what he saw. Here we see a position that he marked in Alipasino Polje where a particular incident occurred. In a moment, we will see the relevant part of Dr. Radinovic's target map for Sarajevo, which will indicate no targets in the area of P8. Perhaps we could go to that. And one can locate the relevant part of the map having regard to the pattern of the streets immediately to the right of the words "Alipasino Polje." Some other general observations in relation to this map: We see number 62 to the right. That appeared twice. Once on Mojmilo hill, as well as here in Alipasino Polje. The list that was tendered with the chart indicated Mojmilo hill, so there is no explanation as to why that should appear again in Alipasino Polje. 101, towards the centre of the screen, according to the supporting document, is simply command post of 102 Motorised Brigade in Alipasino Polje area. No indication as to why it's placed in that part of Alipasino Polje. Indeed, that same command post is shown on other maps as being north of the Miljacka River, but not in this position. The colour of the target according to the colour code of the map should be indicating a mortar or Howitzer position. No explanation as to why it's shown as such, when the document refers to it as a command post. 146 is -- having regard to the document is a position for a 12.7 millimetre machine-gun. No indication as to why it's placed particularly there, and so on. I don't intend to refer to every number on that map. That alone would take an hour. I simply want to give some indication of the degree to which one can and cannot rely upon it without thoroughly checking it. At this point, I make another general observation: Even if it was accurate, even if an incident occurred right alongside a military target, the Defence intimates that it is, therefore, legitimate. It does not offer any further argument as to why that is so. Underlying the distinction between the military target and a legitimate military target are the dual principles, distinction and proportionality. They are the important principles. That is the law. If a civilian, someone, a woman perhaps middle-aged, wearing civilian clothing, is to walk across the entrance to a command headquarters, how does that at all excuse the woman being shot? It doesn't. If a mortar is lobbed from the SRK side to the entrance to the headquarters of the corps, of the ABiH Corps, and as a result only civilians are killed, no evidence of military persons being on the footpath at the time, that is no excuse. That is unlawful. That offends both principles. If there was a mixture of military persons and civilians on the footpath outside the headquarters, the principle of proportionality applies. Was it disproportionate? The overwhelming scheduled and unscheduled incidents, of which there are well over a hundred that we've heard evidence of, typically do not involve any military persons being hit. A classic example is Kosevo Hospital. The Defence has sought to justify return fire to Kosevo Hospital on the basis of it being counterbattery fire. In other words, the ABiH threw mobile mortars, launched mortars from the vicinity, they were merely -- the SRK was merely deploying the well-known military strategy of counterbattery fire, return the fire, neutralise the mortar position. But what is the evidence? The evidence is that time and again, the hospital was hit. Not only by indirect fire such as mortars, but by artillery shells, by tank shells. How could that be explained? The evidence is that the fire was returned long after the mobile mortars are driven off. But there is this most important point of all: Where is the evidence that on any occasion, any ABiH combatants were hit, were neutralised? After 23 months of such action against Kosevo Hospital, there is no evidence of one ABiH combatant being wounded, let alone killed. There is evidence of doctors, of nurses, of patients being killed and wounded, of a critically important civilian facility being damaged at a time when it was most needed, a time of war, in a city virtually under siege. In other words, the principle of proportionality was grossly offended. It was no defence to the accused. Indeed, it was not counterbattery fire; it was retaliatory fire. It was the SRK teaching a lesson to the Bosnian government authorities; namely, you fire at us, we will fire at the hospital. That is the conclusion that the Prosecution respectfully submits one draws from all the evidence. One considers, if it was counterbattery, then ultimately the conclusion we respectfully submit is that it was not. Even if it was, it was disproportionate. I return to the incident at hand that Mr. Ashton gave evidence about. He said that on the 22nd of September, 1992, a shell hit that position in Alipasino Polje where children had been playing. No suggestion on Dr. Radinovic's map of a military target there. The victims were brought to the state hospital. And John Ashton had a close association with the state hospital. He stayed on its exposed and damaged upper floors when he first went to Sarajevo. Ashton saw the victims and photographed them. There was a 6-year-old girl whom he assisted in the treatment of who had a serious arm injury. There was a boy of 9 or 10 who suffered leg injuries resulting in an amputation. Metres away from him at the time were his father and uncle, who were both killed. And he had the misfortune to be conscious when the remains of his father were brought into the hospital on a stretcher, sending him into a state of deep shock. Moving on to the next image, this is not an exhibit. This points out where the PTT building was located. It does it in this fashion because this position is clearly uncontroversial. A number of witnesses marked this location as being the PTT building. A lot of evidence dealt with incidents surrounding and within the PTT building. John Ashton said that in December 1992, about an hour before dark, he observed civilians, particularly old men and women, and quite a few children cutting firewood "right outside the PTT" being shelled. It was a cloudy day, misty and cold, but clear enough to see the hills. And it follows, clear enough for the SRK forces to see the PTT building. Indeed, he could see all the way to the Holiday Inn on that occasion. Three people were killed. Two others carrying wood that they had just cut were wounded. The incident was witnessed by UNHCR and UNPROFOR staff. French UNPROFOR soldiers assisted the victims. Ashton said he was certain that amongst this group there were no soldiers or people wearing military clothing, nothing to indicate the presence of soldiers. The UNPROFOR commander in Sarajevo who witnessed the incident contacted the SRK liaison officer and directed him to stop the shelling, but it continued through the evening. Excuse me, Mr. President. Major Henneberry, the commanding officer of the United Nations military observers on the SRK side, on the 16th of December, 1992, was so concerned at the indiscriminate shelling of the city that he decided he would raise the issue with the accused. And I interpose that evidence at this point because as an example, the incident that John Ashton gave evidence about occurred in December 1992. When Henneberry raised that issue, he protested to the accused that, he said: "The shelling continues, and the rounds landing in the city are not always hitting military targets." He said that the accused vehemently responded that his goal was, to use Henneberry's words, "to either destroy the city or rid it of Muslims." Henneberry said this: "As a soldier, I realised having been there for several months that it was beyond the realm of the feasible for the Serbian forces to be able to destroy the city, to damage it significantly, of course. But to destroy the city, that was not feasible for them." He was disturbed by the barbarism in that comment by the accused. He found it difficult to reconcile that barbarism with the fact that the accused was a well-respected and very intelligent military man. Henneberry said: "There was no doubt of that. He had a commanding presence. He was respected for his military abilities and knowledge by his staff and by the military observers." Henneberry was understandably disturbed by the focus on destroying the city or ridding it of Muslims, to use the accused's words as related by Henneberry. He said that, "They were not in accordance with recognisable rules of conflict. It was somewhat scary. I would have to harken back to the Nuremberg trials where very intelligent men made decisions that were illegal and against the law and caused the death of civilians and military. I recognised and realised that" - what the accused had said - "meant the death of a lot of innocents, innocents which I categorise as the young, the elderly, and the noncombatants. And he was determined to do that." Another point of relevance with the PTT building is that we heard evidence that the ABiH would fire mortars from the vicinity of it, what was called screen firing, quite inappropriate given the fact that it was occupied by the United Nations. General Abdel Razek gave evidence that he complained to the accused about the PTT building being shelled. He said that at first the accused denied it, that he was doing it, and then when confronted with the evidence, he admitted it but said he was doing it because the government forces were firing from it. General -- and he said that they had to stop before I stop, words to that effect.
